title: Spies said 1,400 tanks a month. Statisticians said 246. #shorts
desc:
WWII: intelligence put German tank output at about 1,400 a month. Statisticians, with only the serial numbers of a few captured tanks, said 246. After the war the records showed 245.
How do a few serial numbers count a whole army? Guess in the comments.

Try the method yourself: https://mathparadoxes.com/german-tank-problem
Sources: The Guardian (2006); Ruggles & Brodie, JASA (1947)

title: Almost everyone has more legs than average #shorts
desc:

title: One missing number led to thousands of abortions #shorts
desc:
1995, Britain: an urgent warning says the new contraceptive pills double the risk of blood clots. Many women stop taking the pill; by one estimate the next year brings about 13,000 more abortions in England and Wales. The missing number: about 1 clot in 7,000 women on the old pills, 2 on the new.
Always ask: out of how many?

Relative vs absolute risk: https://mathparadoxes.com/glossary/absolute-vs-relative-risk
Sources: Gigerenzer et al., Psychological Science in the Public Interest (2008); Furedi, Human Reproduction Update (1999)

title: The biggest poll in history picked the wrong president #shorts
desc:
1936: Literary Digest mails 10 million ballots, 2.4 million come back, and it forecasts Alf Landon with 57%. George Gallup asks about 50,000 people and says Roosevelt. Roosevelt takes 60.8% and 46 of 48 states.
How do two million answers lose to fifty thousand? Your guess in the comments.

Who answers decides the result: https://mathparadoxes.com/glossary/sampling-bias

title: Your shuffled deck has never existed before #shorts
desc:

title: Were the bombs on London aimed? #shorts
desc:
1944: Londoners were sure German flying bombs targeted certain districts. Two years later R. D. Clarke split south London into 576 squares and counted 537 hits: the pattern matched pure chance. Randomness looks clumpy.
Next time you see a cluster, ask first: is it just chance?

title: Your A/B test said +24%. The truth: +10% #shorts
desc:
A weak A/B test calls a winner only when noise happens to push the number up, so its wins come out inflated. In our simulation a button that is really 10% better shows about +24% when it wins. Trust the direction, not the number, and size the test before you run it.
How big was your last win, really?

2,000 tests of one button: https://mathparadoxes.com/glossary/statistical-power

title: 20 winning A/B tests: +49% in the report, +7% in reality #shorts
desc:
In our simulation a shop ships 20 winning A/B tests in a year and the report adds up to +49%. A small random holdout group that saw none of the changes shows about +7%. Wins are picked when noise helps, changes chase the same buyer, novelty fades.
What did your year of wins really add?

title: The Hunger Games: run for the Cornucopia, or run away? #shorts
desc:
Sunrise on the Reaping is in cinemas. 24 tributes, 60 seconds on the plate: run for the Cornucopia, or run away? Game theory says some run and some back off, and past a point a richer Cornucopia leaves every tribute worse off.
Then we built the whole arena: build your own tribute and play 2,000 Games. All fives: which start wins most often, the Cornucopia, the edge, or running? Guess in the comments.
